source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Founding claim. Preschoolers do not just play more when evidence is unclear. They pick the one action that splits apart confounded causes. They do this when base rates make the evidence ambiguous, and almost never when the evidence is unambiguous.
numbers: Cognition 120(3):341-349. Mean age 54 months. Two experiments, 20 children per condition.
limits: Toy world only. The authors say they cannot tell if children knew the value of isolating variables at the start or worked it out during the task.
agent_relevance: S7 should fire the splitting test only when the candidate rules are truly tied. If one rule already dominates, a forced test wastes budget.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Formal model used to frame the study: pick the action with the highest expected information gain. Two terms matter: the prior over hypotheses P(H), and the action-to-data map P(D|A,H). The second term only matters when actions cannot isolate variables one to one.
numbers: IG(D,A) = I(P(H|D,A)) - I(P(H)). EIG(A) = sum_i P(D_i|A) IG(D_i,A). P(D_i|A) = sum_k P(D_i|A,H_k) P(H_k). I is Shannon information in bits. Setup: 4 objects of unknown status, only 3 actions (2 single-object, 1 confounded pair).
limits: The model is normative. The authors do not fit it to individual children.
agent_relevance: This is the cleanest formal rule for S7: choose the test with the highest expected entropy drop over the live rules. Our code can compute it exactly for a small rule set.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Experiment 1 design. Children saw that 4 of 4 beads (All Beads) or 2 of 4 beads (Some Beads) turn on a toy. Then two bead pairs both turned it on. One pair came apart. One pair was stuck together. Only the separable pair could be tested one bead at a time.
numbers: 3 conditions (All Beads, Some Beads B, Some Beads AB), 20 children each, N=60. Mean age 54 months.
limits: Contact causality was the assumed folk theory. Children had seen the pulling apart and the one-at-a-time placing during the demonstration, so the target action was familiar.
agent_relevance: Design pattern for a probe: give the agent a base rate that makes new evidence either redundant or ambiguous, then see whether its next test changes.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Experiment 1 result. Almost nobody isolated the beads in the unambiguous condition. About half did so in the ambiguous conditions.
numbers: Informative experiment performed: All Beads 1/20 (5%); Some Beads B 9/20 (45%); Some Beads AB 10/20 (50%). Versus All Beads: chi2(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005 and chi2=10.16, p<.005. The two Some Beads conditions did not differ (chi2=0.10). 65% of All Beads children never pulled the separable pair apart. Coder agreement 95% (kappa .90).
limits: Half of the ambiguous group still did not do it. The effect is selective, not universal.
agent_relevance: Expect even a good explorer to find the splitting test in only about half of cases. Do not read a missed test as a broken scaffold.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Control against the idea that ambiguity just makes children play wildly. The variety of play did not rise in the ambiguous condition. Only the target action rose.
numbers: Mean number of action categories in Experiment 1: All Beads 3.83, Some Beads about 4.06; no significant difference. Experiment 2: 3.00 (Some Beads) vs 2.78 (All Beads), no significant difference. In Experiment 1 one other coded action also differed (63% vs 18%, chi2(1,N=40)=9.37, p<.005); all other comparisons were ns by Fisher exact.
limits: The authors tested each action as a planned comparison with no multiple-comparison correction (alpha .05 uncorrected), on purpose. A critic could press this.
agent_relevance: Selective, not random. Breadth of attempts is not the signal. Whether the attempt separates the live causes is. Score S3 open-mode output on whether candidates separate hypotheses, not on how many were produced.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Experiment 2: children invented the intervention. Only the stuck pair was used. The informative act was to stand the pair on end so only one bead touched the toy. Nobody showed them this.
numbers: N=40, 20 per condition. Informative experiment: All Beads 1/20 (5%); Some Beads 9/20 (45%; 3 who had seen only the second bead activate, 6 who had seen both). chi2(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005. Coder agreement 96%.
quote: The intervention the children discovered was sufficiently non-obvious that it had not initially occurred to the authors of this paper.
limits: Children were wrong about the mechanism: anything pressing the platform worked. Their design fit their folk theory, not the truth.
agent_relevance: A test can be well designed and still rest on a wrong theory. G3 and S7 check the output, not the theory.

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Competing explanations the authors raise: children may have recognised the value of isolating at the start, or inferred it during the task by comparing the base-rate phase with the bead-pair phase. Play also serves other goals (skills, sensation) and varies with temperament and energy.
limits: Not resolved by the data.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, knowing a principle and inferring it from the in-context setup look the same from outside. Test with and without a stated principle.

source: Schulz & Bonawitz (2007) Serious fun: preschoolers engage in more exploratory play when evidence is confounded
finding: Direct precursor. Children play longer with a familiar toy when its causal evidence is confounded, and longer with a new toy when the evidence was clear.
numbers: N=64, mean age 57 months (48-70), 16 per condition, 4 conditions, 60 s free play. More children spent most time on the familiar toy in Confounded than in Matched-for-Effects (chi2(1,N=32)=8.13, p<.01), Matched-for-Trials (6.15, p<.025), No-Independent-Play (4.5, p<.05). Within Confounded, familiar > novel (t(15)=2.79, p<.01). Reversed in Matched-for-Effects (t(15)=3.1, p<.01) and Matched-for-Trials (t(15)=2.48, p=.01). Mean play 27.6 s per toy across conditions.
limits: Published in Developmental Psychology 43(4):1045-1050. I read the author manuscript, not the journal copy.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity is the trigger for returning to an item. A scaffold's trigger for going back and testing again should be a tie in evidence, which G1 already says.

source: Schulz & Bonawitz (2007) Serious fun: preschoolers engage in more exploratory play when evidence is confounded
finding: Three control conditions ruled out boredom with an extra trial, missing independent play, and the pull of simultaneous effects. In the confounded condition 75% of children also moved each lever separately during free play.
numbers: 12 of 16 children (75%) in Confounded moved each lever separately. Total play did not differ across conditions (no main effect). In No Independent Play children played equally long with both toys.
limits: The No-Independent-Play group showed equal play rather than a reversal, so that contrast is weaker than the other two.
agent_relevance: Careful control design is the template for LLM probes: match surface features, vary only ambiguity.

source: Schulz (2012) The origins of inquiry: inductive inference and exploration in early childhood
finding: Schulz's review frames exploration after surprise and after confounding as one Bayesian principle: a learner is uncertain whenever two or more hypotheses have about equal posterior. It lists practices that appear early: explore when evidence is confounded or surprising, isolate candidate causes, use sampling information, weigh teaching against self-exploration.
numbers: Trends Cogn Sci 16(7):382-389. Cites Cook et al.: n=20 per condition, mean 54 months, range 46-64. Also Gweon et al. 2010 (infants 13-18 months) and Denison et al. 2012 (4.5- and 6-month-olds).
limits: The author says no formal model yet produces all and only the epistemic practices of inquiry. Models exist for single practices.
agent_relevance: Supports one rule (uncertainty = tied posteriors) that triggers both look again and split the tie, instead of two separate modules.

source: Schulz (2012) The origins of inquiry: inductive inference and exploration in early childhood
finding: Prior belief changes what children explore. Children with different theories of balance explore differently on identical evidence. Violation of expectation guides exploration through childhood, not only infancy.
numbers: Cites Bonawitz et al. 2012 on balance (see the balance-study lines below for the numbers). Pedagogy study cited as Bonawitz et al. 2011.
limits: Review level. Numbers live in the primary papers.
agent_relevance: Prior theory sets what counts as ambiguous. The same data can be a tie for one agent and not for another, so the tie check must use the agent's own stated rule set.

source: Bonawitz et al. (2011) The double-edged sword of pedagogy: instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery
finding: Teaching narrows exploration. After a teacher showed one function of a toy, children explored less and found fewer of the other functions. An ideal-learner Bayesian model predicts this: a helpful teacher who shows only one function implies there are no others.
numbers: Experiment 1: N=85 preschoolers (Pedagogical plus Interrupted, Naive, Baseline groups of 20 each). Play time: Pedagogical 119.2 s vs Interrupted 179.6, Naive 132.7, Baseline 205.7 (F(1,81)=4.52, p<.05). Unique actions: 4.00 vs 5.30, 5.90, 6.15 (F(1,81)=9.39, p<.01). The toy had four hidden functions.
limits: One toy. The authors say the costs and benefits of instruction have no fully general answer.
agent_relevance: A worked example or a stated plan acts like a teacher and can cut breadth. For open-mode S3, do not show a single worked answer before the agent has made its own spread of candidates.

source: Bonawitz et al. (2011) The double-edged sword of pedagogy: instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery
finding: Direct ostensive cues were neither necessary nor sufficient. Children cut back exploration when they overheard teaching aimed at another child (similar priors), but not when the learner was an adult.
numbers: Experiment 2: N=64, mean 61 months. Direct M=3.13 and Indirect Child M=3.94 action kinds were fewer than Indirect Adult and Intentional (contrast weights +1 +1 -1 -1, linear contrasts significant). Share of play on the demonstrated squeaker: Direct 52%, Indirect Child 60%, Indirect Adult 37%. Total play time did not differ (Direct 70 s, Indirect Child 105, Indirect Adult 84, Intentional 125; F(1,60)=.92, ns).
limits: The authors say parental familiarity could not be fully ruled out. Children learned the demonstrated function equally in the conditions, so only the inference that nothing else exists differed.
agent_relevance: Who an example is for matters. If earlier text looks like a worked solution for this kind of agent, the model may stop searching. G8 and the fresh-context rule in S3 already guard this.

source: Siegel, Magid, Pelz, Tenenbaum, Schulz (2021) Children's exploratory play tracks the discriminability of hypotheses
finding: Children's play time tracks how hard two hypotheses are to tell apart by their own senses. They explore longer when options are harder to discriminate. A noisy-perception (psychophysics) model predicts it.
numbers: Nature Communications 12:3598. Reported N=160, mean 5 years 4 months. Experiments 1-3 (choice): 81.2% (N=16), 79% (N=24), 75% (N=24) correct. Experiments 4-7 (child shakes box; 4 experiments x 4 contrasts, 24 each): model-vs-exploration r=0.95; pooled beta=0.24, 95% CI [0.18, 0.30]. Actual marble count did not predict play (beta=0.0065). Children with positive slope: 19/24, 21/24, 18/24, 19/24.
limits: Methods say 184 recruited and 16 excluded (168), not 160; the gap is not explained. The CI for r is reported as [0.78, 0.95], upper bound equal to the point value, probably a typo. r is across condition means. A simple ratio or difference heuristic fits about as well. No p-values in the main text. Experimenter not blind to box contents. One museum.
agent_relevance: Cook 2011 shows children seek tests that split the cause. Siegel shows they also scale effort to how well a test can split. S7 can scale test effort to rule distinctness: near-twin rules get more probes, clearly different rules get one. Our code can set this from output distance.

source: Bonawitz, van Schijndel, Friel, Schulz (2012) Children balance theories and evidence in exploration, explanation, and learning
finding: Prior theory and evidence interact. Six- and seven-year-olds explore a balanced block more when the evidence contradicts their own theory, and then appeal to a hidden magnet more. Four- and five-year-olds without a theory preferred the novel toy regardless of condition.
numbers: Experiment 1: 95 children aged 6-7 (M=84 months) and 31 aged 4-5 (M=62 months). No-Theory children: novel toy over block F(1,29)=9.43, p<.01, no effect of condition. Theorists: interaction, more play when evidence conflicted with theory, F(1,59)=6.02, p<.05. Mass Theorists with Geometric Center evidence played longer with block than novel toy, t(13)=2.48, p<.05. Center Theorists with Center-of-Mass evidence: t(15)=2.47, p<.05. 11 of 30 (37%) changed predictions after theory-contradicting evidence vs 1 of 30 (3%) after consistent evidence, Fisher p<.01. Explanation interaction chi2(9,N=60)=17.8, p<.05.
limits: Center Theorists did not show the predicted selective appeal to the magnet (50% vs 56%), which the authors blame on age or magnet salience.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity is relative to a held belief. A scaffold with no stated hypothesis cannot be surprised. S2 should write the working rule before S3 so S7 has something to test against.

source: Bonawitz, Lim, Schulz (2007) Weighing the evidence: children's naive theories of balance affect their exploratory play
finding: Earlier conference version of the balance study. No-Theory children preferred the novel toy; classified children's play depended on their beliefs.
numbers: 29 children kept after 6 failed the pretest: 15 Geometric Center, 14 Center of Mass. No-Theory children marginally preferred the novel toy in Geometric Center (t(14)=1.68, p=.057) and significantly in the other condition (t(8)=2.09, p<.05). 69% of No-Theory children gave inconsistent predictions on classification trials.
limits: Small N, conference paper, superseded by the 2012 journal article.
agent_relevance: Supporting only. Cite the journal version for numbers.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) Learning causal overhypotheses through exploration in children and computational models
finding: First direct test of optimal information-gain policies against children on a blicket game. Children took more steps than the ideal agents, yet often stopped before the structure was determined, especially without a hint about the hypothesis space.
numbers: CLeaR 2022. N=85 children aged 4-5. 2x2: conjunctive vs disjunctive x hypothesis space given vs not. Disambiguating data produced: 71% (given) vs 32% (not given), 2-proportion Z test p=0.002. Actions: 14.07 (given) vs 10.58 (not); time 178.65 s vs 195.38 s. Time similar in conjunctive (185.84 s) and disjunctive (187.19 s). Agents (per-step and minimum-step EIG policies) took longer on conjunctive; children did not differ. 11 structures: 7 disjunctive, 4 conjunctive.
limits: Online setting. The ideal models use fixed hypothesis sets; children also tried stochastic and attribute-based ideas the models lack. The authors say children may not maximise information alone. This bounds Cook et al.: selectivity shows in a simple toy, not full optimality in a larger space.
agent_relevance: An exact EIG computation will out-test children in a closed rule set. The risk for the agent lies in a wrong or too small rule set, not in the test choice. Keep the list open to other attributes at S2.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci) answered several classic information-search items like people: it picked the right question type for the Toma lateness case, fell for the congruence bias on an illness-test item, and picked A and 7 on the Wason card task (the normative answer, which most people miss).
numbers: 12 standard vignettes: 6 answered correctly and all 12 correct or human-like (Figure 1B). Small rewordings broke it. Blicket vignette (text description) and an intervention vignette were answered correctly. All 3 Cognitive Reflection Test items got the intuitive wrong answer.
limits: Prompt wording changed answers. The authors warn the canonical tasks may be in the training data (Clever Hans point). One 2022 model. A text blicket case tells the model the evidence, so it does not test spontaneous exploration.
agent_relevance: A vignette pass is weak evidence. S7 probes must use new wording and run the test, not describe it.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: On a real sequential exploration task (the horizon task) GPT-3 did well on reward but did not show the human pattern of exploring more when more trials remain. It also repeated options it had seen more often.
numbers: Mean regret: GPT-3 M=2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans M=3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: no difference from humans (t(5566)=-0.043, p=.97). Long horizon, early: GPT-3 regret lower than humans, t(5550)=-4.07, p<.001; later difference ns (t=-0.75, p=.23). In the unequal-information case it strongly preferred the option it had seen more.
limits: Human data come from Zaller et al. 2021, not collected by the authors. Only two-armed bandits. The authors guess that perseveration comes from next-token prediction.
agent_relevance: The model repeats what it has just seen. For S3 open mode and S7, the order of candidates in context will bias which gets tested. Shuffle in code.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 did not use causal structure when it changed the answer. In the common-cause case it matched interventional inference but did not lower its prediction after observing B=0. In the causal-chain case it gave the same answer as in the common-cause case, unlike people.
numbers: Waldmann and Hagmayer cask task, qualitative comparison to normative and human patterns (Figure 5). No sample counts for the causal items.
limits: Qualitative figures only.
agent_relevance: Cause-structure sensitivity, not test choice alone, was the weak point. Do not rely on the model to say which test separates two causal structures. Compute it from the enumerated rule outputs.

source: Kosoy et al. (2023) Comparing machines and children: developmental psychology experiments to assess LaMDA
finding: LaMDA was scored against children on many developmental tasks. It looked child-like on social and moral items and far from children on causal reasoning, which the authors link to missing self-initiated exploration.
numbers: LLM Response Score (0-5): Social/Moral 4.33; Perception 2.91; Theory of Mind 2.86; Causal Reasoning 1.34. Blicket items from Lucas 2014: not-given-hypothesis conjunctive 1.12, not-given disjunctive 0.44.
limits: Scores are hand ratings on a scale the authors made. One model. Answers may be recalled from papers. Does not follow the human order of developmental difficulty.
agent_relevance: A strong text prior does not give exploration skill. Our scaffold supplies the run-the-test step because the model cannot be trusted to simulate it.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus innovation: what children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet)
finding: Children and adults can find a new use for an everyday object to solve a physical problem. LLMs matched people on picking objects that go together but were much worse at picking the unrelated but useful object. The authors also report that models struggled to extract causal overhypotheses from blicket data (their own work, then in preparation).
numbers: Children 3-7 years (n=42, M age 5.71, SD 1.24) and adults (n=30, M 27.80, SD 5.54). Superficial association: children 88.4% (SE 2.82), adults 84.9% (SE 3.07). Discovering a new function: children 85.2% (SE 3.17), adults 95.7% (SE 1.04). Models tested: gpt-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, Claude, FLAN-T5 XXL, Bloomz; DALLE-2 for images.
limits: Preprint, early models. Exact LLM numbers on the function-discovery part not extracted. The blicket claim cites unpublished work.
agent_relevance: Association is easy for the plain model and innovation is hard. S3 open mode must force a different reading of the object, not just sample again.

source: Gweon & Schulz (2008) Stretching to learn: ambiguous evidence and variability in preschoolers' exploratory play (cited in Cook et al. 2011)
finding: Cited by Cook et al. as showing that preschoolers explore more variably after ambiguous evidence. Not opened this session.
limits: I did not read it. The search budget ran out. Only the citation context is known.
agent_relevance: Pair with the control-line above: breadth may rise after ambiguity, but in Cook et al. breadth was not what produced the informative action.

source: Legare (2012) Exploring exploration: explaining inconsistent information guides hypothesis-testing behavior in young children (cited in Schulz 2012)
finding: Listed in the Schulz review as work on how explaining inconsistent information guides hypothesis testing. Not opened.
limits: Not read. Needed for the replication and extension pass.
agent_relevance: Follow up in the next pass.

source: Lucas et al. (2014) and Gopnik et al. (2017), cited in Kosoy et al. 2022: children learn unusual conjunctive causal rules at least as well as adults
finding: Kosoy et al. cite these for the finding that, given data, children handle conjunctive and disjunctive structures about equally and are more open-minded than adults. Not opened; second hand.
limits: Second hand only.
agent_relevance: A less fixed prior is a possible reason to keep a diverse rule set at S3 and to reduce the pull of the most common rule.
